thread.title: Monarch Casino & Resort: Even Cheaper, Valuation Remains A Concern - Monarch Casino & Resort, Inc. (NASDAQ:MCRI)

author: Vince Martin
title: Monarch Casino & Resort: Even Cheaper, Valuation Remains A Concern - Monarch Casino & Resort, Inc. (NASDAQ:MCRI)
text:
Monarch Casino & Resort ( MCRI ) has one of the better stories in regional gaming. The company's Atlantis resort in Reno is a premier destination in a still-hot market. In Black Hawk (west of Denver), Monarch is serving another in-demand metro area, while the addition of hotel promises a boost to profits starting in the third quarter of 2019.
The combination makes MCRI an attractive takeover target in a space that has consolidated over the past few years. Modest balance sheet leverage, even pro forma for remaining construction spend, gives Monarch options if it chooses to be a buyer rather than a seller. Management seems solid, as both properties consistently have grown market share over the years, while the founding Farahi family still owns 35% of the company.
To top it off, MCRI now is cheaper. The stock touched a 15-month low on Christmas Eve and, even after an 8% bounce, still is down 24% from June highs. Between the story and valuation, MCRI would seem an attractive "buy the dip" candidate for those investors who see the recent sell-off as overdone.
That said, and even with the pullback, the problem remains pretty much what I argued it was a year ago : Monarch looks awfully expensive. MCRI still trades at a substantial premium to the regional gaming sector. And given that multiples have compressed across the space, and that there's no doubt some takeover premium embedded here, MCRI's YTD declines (-16%) have been caused by more than just investor nervousness about the macro cycle. Even not far from the lows, investors are pricing in a substantial amount of growth, and an enormous boost from the hotel in Black Hawk. As it did a year ago, that looks too optimistic.
The MCRI Bull Case Again, from a qualitative standpoint, this is an attractive story. The Reno economy was late in recovering from the financial crisis but has benefited from a boom the last few years to the point that affordable housing has become a problem . Reno has become a tech hotspot thanks to investments from Apple ( AAPL ), Tesla ( TSLA ), and many others. Visitation has returned to pre-crisis levels .
As a result, gaming market growth has been solid. Over the twelve months ending November, according to Nevada state figures , the six Reno casinos with over $36 million in revenue saw gaming revenue rise 5.87%. Hotel and food and beverage appear strong as well; changes in revenue recognition of comps skew the figures, but occupancy was up 1.5 points in Q3 (and flat YTD), while RevPAR (revenue per available room) appears to have grown on an organic basis.
Meanwhile, Monarch's Atlantis is one of the premier properties in the market - and has seen a number of improvements in recent years. As Reno has grown, and more affluent citizens have moved toward the south Reno area, Atlantis' share has grown consistently:
Source: Monarch Casino investor presentation , October 2018
Meanwhile, in 2012, Monarch acquired the bankrupt Riviera casino in Black Hawk, Colorado, about an hour west of Denver. It's investing an estimated $430-442 million into renovating the property and adding a hotel tower that should be completed in the third quarter of 2019.
That property, too, serves a booming economy . Black Hawk, including neighboring Central City, is one of two gaming enclaves in the entire state, and expansion efforts have been voted down repeatedly (and resoundingly), most recently in 2014 . Monarch has argued that the Black Hawk market is underserved in terms of hotel rooms, with the only other high-end integrated resort being the Ameristar (now owned by Penn National Gaming ( PENN ) after its acquisition of Pinnacle closed in October).
Here, too, Monarch has taken market share, according to its investor presentation, despite disruption from ongoing construction in the casino and outside. It has a premier location, being the first property seen on the way in from Denver. And here, too, Monarch has exposure to one of the better gaming markets in the country. The hotel should add ancillary revenue and drive visitation and gaming revenue.
So, there are two highly attractive properties. What there aren't - at least not anymore - are much in the way of acquisition targets left in the gaming space. There's multi-billion-dollar Penn National, Eldorado Resorts ( ERI ), Caesars Entertainment ( CZR ) and Boyd Gaming ( BYD ). Below that level is mostly private or small-cap public companies with varying degrees of exposure to substandard markets and/or properties that are too small for the majors to deal with. Qualitatively, Monarch without question is the best acquisition target in the market, with maybe Empire Resorts ( NYNY ) as the only other pure resort play left for the majors to buy. And so any dip - particularly the 20%+ drop since this summer - could look like a buying opportunity.
The Valuation Problem The problem is that the bull case here isn't exactly hidden. Reno's growth is such that it made the New York Times . Seemingly everyone either is moving to Denver or knows someone who is. Consolidation in the gaming space has been going on for some time.
And that bull case certainly looks priced in under all but the most aggressive assumptions. Coming out of Q3, Monarch's trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA is $59.8 million, implying a 12.3x EV/EBITDA multiple. That's an enormous multiple for the gaming space. As I've pointed out before, Pinnacle paid 7.6x for Ameristar back in 2012. Admittedly, that was a good deal: Pinnacle sold itself for 10x+ pre-synergies. (The figure was 6.6x after synergies, per the Penn acquisition presentation ; adding back the synergies gets to 10.7x. I'd note the complexity of that deal, including divestitures and sale leasebacks with Gaming & Leisure Partners ( GLPI ), muddies the waters a bit in terms of fully trusting that 10x figure. I'd add that PENN stock is down 37% since the day before it announced the Pinnacle acquisition.)
But this is a sector where double-digit EV/EBITDA multiples are rare - and usually dangerous. Valuations hit that market in 2006-2007, only to tumble. And the same phenomenon has played out (albeit in a much less severe way) over the past few months:
BYD data by YCharts
BYD now trades at 8.4x (based on 2018 guidance), after clearing 10x. ERI admittedly has held up well, trading at 10x+ pro forma 2018 EBITDA after its acquisition of Tropicana Entertainment, though its multiple has come down well over a turn this quarter. There are so many moving parts at PENN and CZR as to make pinning down an EV/EBITDA (or EV/EBITDAR) multiple close to impossible, but the move in those equities shows that multiples at least have compressed there as well.
And, again, because one possible endgame for Monarch is a sale, that compression matters even ignoring the higher likelihood of macro trouble being discounted by the broad market. It's easier for an acquirer to pay 11x or 12x EBITDA for an acquisition (particularly given potential synergies at the corporate level) with a stock valued at 10x+ than with one at 8x+. And so, it's impossible to disentangle MCRI's valuation from that of peers for reasons that go beyond simple comparisons.
Obviously, that 12.3x figure needs to be adjusted for the pending hotel. Per the Q3 release, Monarch has $169-176 million in remaining spend in Black Hawk, which isn't going to be covered (or close) by free cash flow over the next three quarters. Pro forma for the midpoint of that spend, the enterprise value here moves up to a little over $900 million, putting EV/EBITDA at 15x+.
That spend - and the $266 million spent so far - obviously have some ROI, and will boost EBITDA as well. But the long-running concern - and admittedly, I didn't like the expansion when Monarch announced it three years ago; MCRI has nearly doubled - is that even a big boost from the hotel isn't enough to get that multiple to a comfortable range. At the risk of using round numbers, I'd still argue that it's tough (and unwise) to pay 10x+ for pretty much any gaming stock, no matter how well-positioned. Particularly in this market, and after the recent treatment of PENN stock post-Pinnacle, that seems a reasonable rule of thumb.
To get there on a pro forma basis, Black Hawk needs to add something close to $25 million in EBITDA, even giving some credit for cash flow over the next three quarters. Monarch stopped breaking out property-level figures after 2013, but my guess would be that a $25 million increase would require a roughly doubling of profits.
It's a big ask. And to reiterate a past point, even though that figure has come down over time (in part due to lower stock price of late, and EBITDA growth before that), the Ameristar case study that Monarch itself uses suggests the company might be able to get there:
Source: Monarch investor presentation, October 2018
After opening its hotel, Ameristar added $23.3 million in EBITDA. But there's some points to note here. First, in 2009, Colorado's Amendment 50 also passed. That allowed for a dramatic expansion in table game limits from $5 (yes, five dollars) to $100, which helped gaming revenue growth. So, too, did the recovery from the financial crisis (which was tepid in some places nationwide, but rather quick and strong in the Denver metro).
And, of course, Ameristar's expansion created the first true resort in Black Hawk. Its hotel towers over the area. (Central City, to which one can walk from Black Hawk, put in zoning to require casinos to maintain the look and feel of the 'old' downtown and thus stay much smaller. In part due to that move, its gaming revenue is less than one-eighth that of Black Hawk.) The Black Hawk gaming market is bigger, admittedly, but perhaps not that much bigger: GGR in fiscal 2018 was up about 12% from fiscal 2010. (Colorado fiscal years end June 30.)
Even back at $37, a roaring success already looks priced in. If Monarch matches the success of Ameristar on a dollar basis ($23 million-plus) - with entrenched competition and no regulatory tailwinds - it's still trading above 10x pro forma EBITDA. That's not a hugely attractive multiple. The figure still is almost exactly 10x assuming ~$7 million in synergies (3% of revenue).
And so, the problem remains in terms of supporting the valuation. There are basically three ways to upside:
Monarch sells itself for (or continues to trade at) a multiple that would be one of the highest ever recorded in the industry; The hotel expansion adds more profit than did Ameristar, whose resort quite literally changed the face of Black Hawk; and/or higher earnings in Reno or through inorganic efforts allows the company to grow into, and eventually beyond, the current valuation concerns. I'm simply not that confident on any of those fronts to see MCRI as compelling - or truthfully even all that attractive.
How This Plays Out As far as the acquisition goes, it's worth noting that a sale isn't quite that simple. Eldorado - another family-owned, Reno-based operator - would seem to make some sense. But ERI already has two properties in Black Hawk, including the Isle of Capri next door. Boyd could make some sense, but it's spent its big-money dollars in Las Vegas (Cannery and the Aliante in 2016) and got a cut-rate deal (6.25x EBITDA pre-synergies) in picking up divested regionals from Penn. Caesars probably isn't buying anyone else any time soon.
I'm skeptical there's going to be some sort of bidding war for Monarch, even if it is the most attractive asset on the market. Churchill Downs ( CHDN ) probably is the best buyer, given its clear interest in growing its casino business (Monarch could open the western U.S.) and a high valuation of its own that can support paying up. Still, in this market and nine months ahead of the hotel opening in Black Hawk, I doubt anyone will be in any rush to pay a double-digit multiple. That's what it takes to see upside in 2019 and perhaps even into 2020 barring a major growth acceleration in Reno over the next five quarters.
As for hotel expansion-driven growth, we'll see. But I'd point out that Black Hawk, as a market, hasn't been quite the growth engine that the booming Denver feeder market would suggest. GGR did grow 2.9% in fiscal 2018. But that followed a sub-1% increase in 2017, and per the state of Colorado's Gaming Updates , market-wide gaming revenue has declined 1.3% in the first four months of fiscal 2019. The market likely does need hotel rooms and Monarch could help grow the market on its own. But even a bullish outlook still suggests that the market growth rate isn't moving the needle here: it's all about share. And Monarch will need to take substantial share to ~double profits in Black Hawk: Ameristar got to 28% at one point, while Monarch's Q2 share (according to the investor presentation) was under 13%.
Acquisition and expansion aside, there's still some good news, admittedly. Performance doesn't look spectacular of late: for the year, revenue is up 3.4%, with casino revenue (excluding accounting) rising 2.8% and Adjusted EBITDA climbing 3.7%. SG&A has deleveraged, owing to unsurprising wage pressure. In the context of regional gaming, that performance looks reasonably solid, particularly given cited lower hold at Atlantis and construction in Colorado. In the context of a double-digit EBITDA multiple, however, even with those headwinds that growth doesn't seem like quite enough.
Monarch could spark that growth through an acquisition. Even a conservative outlook toward hotel-driven profit increases still suggests a low-2x leverage multiple pro forma (something like $180 million in debt, backing out NTM cash flow, against a base of $80 million in Adjusted EBITDA). Monarch could lever up to 4x even in a rising-rate environment, and a cash-and-stock deal could increase its buying power.
But, on this side, too, there's a problem in terms of what deal actually makes sense. Smaller public operators like Full House Resorts ( FLL ) and Nevada Gold ( UWN ) bring much weaker assets into the portfolio. The same is true of private options like Affinity Gaming, now owned by PE firm Z Capital, which makes some sense from a geographic standpoint (Black Hawk, metro Reno, Vegas, and three Midwestern regionals as a beachhead for expansion), and Jacobs Entertainment, which has two properties in Black Hawk and the Sands Regency in downtown Reno.
The one target that would be interesting - and Monarch has floated the idea of growing through M&A in its limited public commentary - is Golden Entertainment ( GDEN ). Golden's distributed gaming routes in Montana and Nevada have real value. A tie-up with Monarch could accelerate the growth of its pub business into the Reno metro. Golden owns the Stratosphere in Las Vegas, which could benefit from some Atlantis-style management. And its casino in Maryland could allow Monarch to start expanding beyond the West.
Even that deal isn't perfect, however - and it still pairs Monarch's hugely attractive assets with Golden's mixed portfolio. (Does the combined company pique interest from one of the majors in the Laughlin and Pahrump properties, for instance?)
And that highlights the qualitative issue here: what looks like an enormously attractive story at first glance has some concerns underneath. MCRI seems a natural takeover target - but who, exactly, is buying it, when, and what price? The two properties would seem a nice base to follow Eldorado's hugely successful M&A strategy - but there are many fewer attractive assets out there than there were in 2012. Organic growth has been solid - but not quite spectacular, and cyclical concerns have to weigh.
Add to that a still-substantial premium in terms of valuation, and the plethora of cyclical "buy the dip" candidates beyond the sector, and the story at MCRI doesn't look all that compelling. If Black Hawk disappoints next year and/or if multiples come down to levels more in line with historical takeout valuations, the stock still has quite a bit of a potential downside ahead. It's difficult to find a path to enough upside to take that risk - or choose MCRI over other stocks in the sector and beyond who have fallen just as far.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions.
